Nevertheless, lexical stress is by no means free: indeed, conceptually it is the same as in Swedish. ... sweep_summary: Tavringer Romani (tavr1235) is not in the catalog. The single Glottolog title-hit, Bruce 1998 'Allmän och svensk prosodi', is a textbook of general and Swedish prosody; Glottolog's own record says its link to Tavringer Romani is a 'computerized assignment from "svensk"', and Libris subject headings are Prosodi / Svenska språket — relevance: other language (Swedish), no open copy, priority none (its 2012 edition is however what Carling et al. cite for the Swedish stress facts). Beyond the listed item, this search of works with stress in the title obtained two works from the per-language bibliography: (1) Carling, Lindell & Ambrazaitis 2014, Scandoromani (Brill), §2.5.1 'Lexical Stress' — read via overlapping Google Books snippets assembled into a continuous passage: one primary stress per simplex word; by default initial stress in di-/trisyllabic words as in Swedish; exceptions with second-syllable stress in some Romani-origin nouns (kerál, manúsch, maskán, molvína, with initial-stress variants), Swedish-prefixed verbs (för-móllvra, fursté) and some unprefixed verbs (ragústa); no stress minimal pairs; chapter summary: 'lexical stress is adapted — as is quantity — to the Scandinavian system of initial stress but with exceptions'; Swedish-type Accent I/II pitch accent also present. Full text paywalled (Brill CAPTCHA; Harvard print copy exists) — high priority to acquire for page numbers and Table 2.13. (2) Lindbäck 2020 (Uppsala BA thesis, open, downloaded from an Internet Archive copy because DiVA refused connections): segmental phonology only; says vowel quantity is distributed as in Standard Swedish where stress and length coincide and that suprasegmentals came from Swedish, but gives no stress-placement rule. Best new statement: Carling et al. 2014 §2.5.1 (snippet-level access). and gbooks_searchwithin/ appeared in that directory during this search of works with stress in the title from another process and were not read or catalogued here; was created by this search of works with stress in the title at 11:11 UTC (none existed at 10:52 UTC).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Swedish Romani (Scandoromani) has taken over the Scandinavian system: every simplex word carries one primary stress and it falls on the initial syllable, together with Swedish-type quantity and the Swedish tonal word accents (Accent I / Accent II) on the stressed syllable. There are lexical exceptions of several types, the first being frozen forms with inherited Romani non-initial stress (e.g. the frozen infinitive te avél 'to be'); p. 58 shows doublets with initial stress (Accent II) vs final stress (Accent I) for the same word, e.g. ['ma:noʃ] vs [ma'noʃ:]. Some compounds carry main stress on the second element regardless of the members' own stress (bèddo-kher).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not visible in the snippets. Compound stress: main stress on the second element in a class of compounds (p. 53, bèddo-kher 'mansion'), paralleled with Swedish glasmäste'ri (p. 50); the grave accent on bèddo marks the non-primary first element.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 62 lists several exception types to initial stress; type 1 = frozen forms with retained Romani final stress (te avél 'to be'); the next type begins 'Culture..' (cut off in the snippet; presumably culture/loan words). p. 58: variants with initial stress take Accent II, variants with final stress Accent I. p. 76: individual, dialectal and family-lectal variation in the distribution of stress and pitch accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('every Swedish Romani simplex word'); citation forms with tonal accent measured in Figure 2.2; data are Swedish Romani (the Swedish side of Scandoromani). Access was Google Books search-inside snippets, so surrounding sentences (the full exception list, any secondary-stress statement) are unseen.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is about Swedish Romani (svensk romani / resanderomani), the Swedish side of Scandoromani; Glottolog tavr1235 'Tavringer Romani' covers both the Swedish and Norwegian (tavring) varieties, and no accessible source states the Norwegian pattern (Iversen 1944 has a stress section but is Norway-only online). Lindbäck 2020 describes one speaker's idiolect and is silent on stress.

new_statements.reading: Fixed word stress on the first syllable by default (Swedish-type initial stress, with Swedish-type Accent I/II pitch accent anchored on the stressed syllable), with lexical exceptions: some nouns of Romani origin keep or vary toward second-syllable stress (kerál, manúsch, maskán, molvína), Swedish-prefixed verbs and a few unprefixed verbs are stressed on the second syllable as in Swedish. No stress minimal pairs, but stress is contrastive in principle. This is a first-hand description by the authors with speaker/co-author Lenny Lindell, read only through Google Books snippets that were overlapped into a continuous passage; the full chapter is paywalled at Brill.

sources.note: First-hand description (speaker LL = co-author Lenny Lindell, with F0 measurements). Every simplex word has one primary stress; no stress minimal pairs exist, but stress is not free and is 'as phonemically important in Swedish Romani as in Swedish'. Default: initial stress in di- and trisyllabic words (as in Swedish). Exceptions: second-syllable stress in some nouns (kerál, manúsch, maskán, molvína — with initial-stress variants), Swedish-prefixed verbs stressed on the second syllable like their Swedish models (för-móllvra, fursté), and some unprefixed verbs (ragústa, variable).
